# OROS NVGate Developer Framework

> Generated 2026-08-25. Framework version: 17.00.002 113362-061272-240806-1502
> This file tells an AI assistant what to read, in what order, and what to trust.

## Layout

    llms.txt        this file
    AI/             machine-readable references, generated from the official manuals
    Framework/      the official OROS Framework, byte for byte, never modified

Paths below are relative to the folder holding this file.

## Start here

NVDrive is a **TCP/IP command language** for NVGate and OROS 3-series analyzers.
Connect to host `127.0.0.1`, port `3000`. NVGate must be running and in connected
mode before any command is sent.

Two separate capability layers, do not confuse them:

- **Live control** — the `pynvdrive` Python library, or raw NVDrive commands over TCP.
  Requires NVGate to be running. Use it to start/stop measurements, change settings,
  read live results, react to events.
- **File access** — the `orostk.file` module and the C++ DLLs. Does not require
  NVGate. Use it to read or write saved signals and results on disk.

Two practical notes:

- `pynvdrive` is ready to use at `Framework/Python/pynvdrive/pynvdrive/`, with 21
  worked examples next to it in `Framework/Python/pynvdrive/examples/`.
- `orostk` is **not** ready to use: it ships as installable archives in
  `Framework/Python/NVFileManager/Packages/` (one per Python version, e.g.
  `OROSPythonToolkit_Python312_x64_bdist.zip`). Install the one matching your
  interpreter before importing it. Its own examples are in
  `Framework/Python/NVFileManager/OROSPythonToolkit_examples.zip`.
- `orostk` spans both layers: `orostk.file` is offline, but `orostk.nvdrive` is a
  **live** client and carries the notification framework. Do not assume `orostk`
  means offline.

## Structured references — read these first

These are machine-readable and are the fastest path to a correct answer.

- `AI/HOWTO_NVDrive_from_Python.md` - **start here for writing code.** A short guide
  with working `pynvdrive` examples: connect, run, read a setting, fetch a result,
  react to the operator, and the traps that cost the most time. The reference files
  below tell you what exists; this one tells you how it is done.

- `AI/nvdrive_commands.json` — one record per NVDrive command: syntax, parameters
  (marked required or optional), return value, error codes, examples, and the
  `pynvdrive` block. **Check it before writing Python**: when `pynvdrive` is `null`,
  no Python class exists and the command must be sent directly (a two-line call, see
  the HOWTO section 7bis). When it is present it carries the import line, the class
  name, the constructor arguments in order, and the attribute the reply lands on - so
  you never have to guess a method name or a keyword.
- `AI/nvdrive_errors.json` — every error code, its meaning, and the command that
  produces it. Tell the two kinds apart by the **spacing**, not the length: consistency
  codes come as three spaced groups (`188 001 000`), execution codes as one unspaced
  run (`000008000`). Both are nine digits. The first group identifies the command, so
  the same message can carry different codes: "Setting unknown" is `188 001 000` from
  `GetSettingInfo` but `028 001 000` from `SetSettingValue`.
- `AI/nvgate_notifications.json` — the 79 notifications NVGate can
  send you when the operator changes something, each with its command id and the
  typed properties that follow in the received block. **Read this before writing any
  event-driven code**: `pynvdrive` has no wrapper for this family at all, so the
  register commands must be sent raw.
- `AI/nvdrive_result_ids.json` — the numbers that address a result: 20 module ids,
  128 process ids, plus unit and operator codes. **Read this before trying to fetch a
  result.** Its `quantity_map` goes straight from what you want to the address:
  an averaged spectrum is module 10 (FFT1), process 2 (AVERAGE SPECTRUM); an overall
  level is module 2 (MONITOR), process 10 (RMS). These tables are in the manual too,
  but printed apart from their headings, so searching the Markdown for them misleads.
- `AI/dll_api.json` — the 1251 exported entry points of the NVGate DLLs, with
  typed parameters, taken from the public C++ headers. Use it when driving NVGate
  from C++, C# or Visual Basic instead of Python.
- Markdown mirrors of four of the five official manuals, for anything the structured
  files do not cover. The fifth, `Framework/Matlab/MatDrive_Reference_Manual.pdf`,
  covers the MATLAB toolbox and is not mirrored: this kit covers the Python and C++
  routes. `<!-- page N -->` markers map back to the corresponding PDF:
  `AI/NVDrive_Reference_Manual.md`, `AI/NVGate_Notification_Mechanism.md`,
  `AI/DLL_NVDCommand_and_NVDResult_Reference_Manual.md`,
  `AI/OR3x_Developer_Toolkit.md`.
- `AI/nvgate_idn_catalog.json` - 756 setting identifiers, each with
  both forms of the IDN, the label NVGate shows for it, and its type. This is how you
  turn "the range of input 3" into something you can actually send. A submodule
  ending in a number is one member of a family: the file lists `frontEnd.input1`, and
  `frontEnd.input3.label` works exactly the same way, only the number changes.
  That rule holds for the **text** form. The legacy numbering of family members is not
  always regular, so do not compute a legacy triplet for member N: use the text form,
  or ask NVGate with Shift + right-click.
  Where NVGate has no name for a submodule it keeps a number and an index, as in
  `dynamicOperating.674:1.label`; where it has none for a setting, the setting keeps
  its number, as in `dynamicOperating.channel1.447`. Both forms are valid - the `name`
  field tells you what they are ("Label", "Coef.").

## Source of truth, in order

1. The structured JSON files in `AI/`.
2. `Framework/NVDrive_Reference_Manual.pdf` (386 pages) — the official specification.
3. The working examples: `Framework/Python/pynvdrive/examples/` (21 scripts,
   including `example_markers.py`, `example_getresult.py` and `example_setsettings.py`),
   and `Framework/Visual/Examples/` (39 C++ files). Examples are often more
   reliable than prose for getting a call right.
4. The library sources: `Framework/Python/pynvdrive/pynvdrive/` (161 distinct
   command classes), and `orostk` once you have installed it from `Packages/`.
5. C++ headers: `Framework/Visual/include/` (14 public headers) — the real DLL
   signatures, with Doxygen comments. The example projects carry further private
   headers; the public API is the one under `Framework/Visual/include/`.

## Setting identifiers (IDNs)

A setting is addressed by an IDN. The modern form is text:

    frontEnd.input1.label
    recorder.track1.source
    fft1.channel1.inputFilter

The legacy form is a triplet of numbers (`1.3.1`), still accepted but limited to 32
channels. Many commands take three parameters for the IDN; pass `""` for the ones you
do not use, so the parameter count stays correct:

    SetSettingValue frontEnd input3 label example
    SetSettingValue frontEnd.input3.label "" "" example
    SetSettingValue 1 3 1 example

In NVGate, Shift + right-click on a setting reveals its IDN, in both forms.

## Traps worth knowing

- **A setting may not take effect immediately.** This is the single most common
  false alarm: you write a setting, the command returns success, and nothing appears
  to change. Some settings apply at once, others only once the analysis is restarted.
  Restart the analysis before concluding that the command failed.
- **Not every documented command has a Python wrapper.** 145 of the
  manual's 309 command sections are wrapped by `pynvdrive`; the remaining
  164 must be sent as raw commands over TCP.
  Most of the marker family falls in that category: of the 43 commands in the Marker
  category, **8 have a wrapper and 35 do not** - `AddHarmonicMarker`, `AddMaxMarker`
  and `AddSideBandMarker` are among the 35. Check the field on the command you
  actually want, never assume either way, and never invent a Python method name.
  See `AI/HOWTO_NVDrive_from_Python.md` section 7 for how to send an unwrapped
  command - it is a two-line call, not socket programming.
- **Notifications are the only way to react to the operator**, and they need more
  than a register command. Your own process must run a TCP server and tell NVGate to
  connect back to it with `ConnectToTCPClient` - without that, you register
  successfully and then wait forever. `orostk.nvdrive.notification_reader` does all of
  this for you, once `orostk` is installed from `Packages/`; a runnable example is in
  `Framework/Python/NVFileManager/OROSPythonToolkit_examples.zip`, folder
  `example_notification/`. Decode what you
  receive against `AI/nvgate_notifications.json`.
- **What is visible depends on which plug-ins are active.** A setting can exist and
  still be unreadable because its module is inactive. `GetSettingInfo` reports this in
  its third and fifth returned strings.
- **There is no `GetSettingList` command.** You cannot enumerate the settings of a
  sub-module over NVDrive. `GetSubModuleList` returns sub-module IDNs, and
  `GetSettingInfo` describes one setting at a time, but nothing lists them all.
- **Prefer NVGate's own computation.** FFT, 1/n-octave, order tracking, FRF, overall
  levels, waterfall and Campbell diagrams are all computed by NVGate. Drive it and
  fetch the result rather than reimplementing the maths.

## Do not rely on

- `initasb.ini` and `process.ini` in the NVGate installation folder (not part of
  this kit). Nothing in `AI/` is derived from them. Both open with a
  comment stating they are no longer used. They still contain useful metadata, but
  they are not maintained and must not be treated as a specification.
- The generated HTML documentation trees as a primary source. They are complete but
  very noisy to parse; the structured files above carry the same information.
